title: Contains Duplicate — check using HashSet in O(n).
shortTitle: Contains Duplicate — Check Using a HashSet in O(n)

s1_definition.profdef: The contains-duplicate problem asks whether any value appears more than once in a collection. The efficient solution scans the collection once, adding each element to a HashSet; the HashSet's add method returns false when the element is already present, so the first time add returns false you have found a duplicate and return true. This runs in average linear time because HashSet operations are average constant time, using linear extra space for the set.

A clerk keeps a box of identifiers already seen and drops each new identifier in; the moment an identifier is already in the box, the clerk shouts "duplicate" and stops. Checking the box is near-instant, so the whole batch is cleared in one quick pass.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The contains-duplicate problem asks whether any value appears more than once in a collection. The efficient solution scans the collection once, adding each element to a HashSet; the HashSet's add method returns false when the element is already present, so the first time add returns false you have found a duplicate and return true. This runs in average linear time because HashSet operations are average constant time, using linear extra space for the set.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India processes a batch of transaction identifiers and must be sure none was submitted twice, because a duplicate identifier means a transaction could be applied twice and Rajesh could be charged twice. A clerk keeps a box of identifiers already seen and drops each new identifier in; the moment an identifier is already in the box, the clerk shouts "duplicate" and stops. Checking the box is near-instant, so the whole batch is cleared in one quick pass.

**One line to remember:** Add each element to a HashSet; the first time add returns false you have a duplicate.

sections.s2_technical:
A HashSet stores unique elements and offers average constant-time add and contains, because it hashes each element to a bucket. The neat part is that add returns a boolean: true if the element was newly added and false if it was already present. So you do not even need a separate contains call; you loop over the collection, call add on each element, and if add ever returns false you immediately return true for contains-duplicate. If the loop finishes with every add returning true, there were no duplicates and you return false.

This is average linear time. Each add is average constant time, and you do one per element, so the total is linear in the number of elements. The trade-off is linear extra space for the set, which is the classic time-for-space exchange: you spend memory to avoid the N log N cost of sorting or the quadratic cost of comparing every pair.

A senior point is the alternatives and when they win. If you are allowed to mutate and sort the input, sorting first then scanning adjacent equal elements finds duplicates in N log N time with no extra set, which is better when memory is tight. The brute-force double loop comparing every pair is quadratic and only acceptable for tiny inputs. The HashSet approach is the right default when you want the fastest average time and can afford the memory.

Another senior point is correctness of equality and hashing. The HashSet relies on the elements implementing equals and hashCode consistently. For your own identifier class you must override both, and they must agree, otherwise the set may treat equal identifiers as different and miss duplicates. For BigDecimal there is a famous trap: BigDecimal equals also considers scale, so one and one point zero are not equal and hash differently, which means a HashSet would not treat them as duplicates even though they are numerically equal. If numeric duplication is what matters, I normalise the scale first or key on the stripped value.

A third point is early exit. Returning the moment the first duplicate is found avoids scanning the rest, which on a large batch with an early duplicate saves real time. I also size the HashSet with an expected capacity when I know the input size, to avoid rehashing as it grows.

A small finance-domain example: `Set<String> seen = new HashSet<>(ids.length * 2); for (String id : ids) { if (!seen.add(id)) return true; } return false;` returns true as soon as a repeated transaction id appears.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India receives a batch of transaction identifiers to apply to accounts, and applying the same identifier twice would double-charge a customer like Rajesh. Before processing, the batch must be checked for any repeated identifier, and because batches are large the check must be fast and must stop at the first duplicate. Detecting a duplicate with a HashSet in one pass is exactly this guard.

This is exactly how contains-duplicate works in Java — we add each identifier to a set and the first time add returns false we have found a repeat.

Problem 2 — Some identifiers are numeric amounts stored as BigDecimal where numerically equal values could carry different scale, so a naive HashSet of BigDecimal would miss numeric duplicates. The check must normalise the scale so that numerically equal values are treated as duplicates, demonstrating awareness of the BigDecimal equals-and-hashCode trap.

What the code will do: a `DuplicateGuard` with `hasDuplicate(String[] ids)` using a pre-sized HashSet and early exit, plus `hasNumericDuplicate(BigDecimal[] amounts)` that strips trailing zeros so numeric equality is honoured. The demo checks a clean batch, a batch with a repeated id, and numerically equal amounts.


sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the duplicate batch is `TXN-001, TXN-002, TXN-001`.

Step 1: `hasDuplicate` checks the length; three elements is enough. We create a HashSet pre-sized to twice the length to avoid rehashing as it fills.

Step 2: We add `TXN-001`. The set was empty, so add returns true, meaning it was newly inserted, no duplicate yet.

Step 3: We add `TXN-002`. It was not present, so add returns true again. The set now holds two identifiers.

Step 4: We add `TXN-001` again. It is already in the set, so add returns false. That false is our signal: we log the duplicate and return true immediately, without looking at any further elements. This early exit is what saves time on large batches.

Step 5: For the clean batch, every add returns true, the loop completes, and the method returns false, meaning no duplicates.

Step 6: For the numeric check, we add the stripped form of `100`, which is a canonical value, then we add the stripped form of `100.00`, which strips to the same canonical value, so add returns false and we report a numeric duplicate. Without stripping, BigDecimal equals would treat them as different because of scale and we would miss the duplicate.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T17:00:00Z INFO No duplicate identifiers in batch
2026-10-26T17:00:00Z INFO Clean batch has duplicate? false
2026-10-26T17:00:00Z WARNING Duplicate transaction id detected: TXN-001
2026-10-26T17:00:00Z INFO Dup batch has duplicate? true
2026-10-26T17:00:00Z WARNING Numeric duplicate amount detected: 100.00
2026-10-26T17:00:00Z INFO Numerically equal amounts duplicate? true
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [TXN-001, TXN-002, TXN-001]
    │
    ▼
  HashSet seen (pre-sized)
    │ add TXN-001 → true (new)
    │ add TXN-002 → true (new)
    │ add TXN-001 → false (present) → DUPLICATE → early exit
    ▼ true
  Numeric path: [100, 100.00]
    │ stripTrailingZeros → both canonical → add false → duplicate
    ▼ true
  Output: duplicate batch rejected before processing
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The contains-duplicate problem asks whether any value appears more than once, and the fast solution is a single pass with a HashSet. I add each element to the set, and because HashSet's add returns false when the element is already present, the first time add returns false I have found a duplicate and return true. If every add succeeds, there are no duplicates. It is average linear time because HashSet operations are average constant time, at the cost of linear extra memory for the set.

I always weigh the trade-off. The HashSet approach spends memory to get the fastest average time, which is the right default. If memory is tight and I may mutate the input, sorting first and scanning adjacent equal elements finds duplicates in N log N with no extra set, and the brute-force double loop is quadratic and only fine for tiny inputs.

The correctness point I stress is equality and hashing. HashSet depends on equals and hashCode being consistent, so for my own identifier types I override both. For BigDecimal there is a famous trap: equals also considers scale, so one hundred and one hundred point zero zero are not equal and hash differently, which means a plain HashSet would miss that numeric duplicate. When numeric equality is what matters I normalise the scale first, for example by stripping trailing zeros, before putting values in the set.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to guard a batch of transaction identifiers before applying them, because a repeated identifier could double-charge a customer like Rajesh. The guard pre-sizes the set, exits at the first duplicate, and for numeric amounts normalises scale so numerically equal values are caught. Explaining the add-returns-false trick, the memory trade-off, and the BigDecimal equals trap shows the interviewer that I know the efficient solution and the subtle correctness issues that bite in real financial data.
